verses.text: Jesus left that place and went to his hometown, with his disciples following.
On the Sabbath he began teaching in the synagogue. Many who heard him were amazed. “Where did he get all this?” they asked. “What’s this wisdom he’s been given? How can he do such powerful works?
Isn’t he the carpenter, Mary’s son, and the brother of James, Joses, Judas, and Simon? Aren’t his sisters here with us?” And they took offense at him.
Jesus told them, “A prophet is honored everywhere except in his hometown, among his relatives, and in his own household.”
He couldn’t do any mighty works there, except lay his hands on a few sick people and heal them.
He was amazed at their unbelief. Then he went around the villages teaching.
Jesus called the Twelve and began sending them out two by two. He gave them authority over impure spirits.
He instructed them to take nothing for the journey except a walking stick—no bread, bag, or money in their belts.
They could wear sandals, but weren’t to take an extra shirt.
He said, “Whenever you enter a house, stay there until you leave that place.

If a place won’t welcome you or listen to you, leave and shake the dust off your feet as a warning to them. I’m telling you, it’ll be better for Sodom and Gomorrah on judgment day than for that town.”
So they went out and preached that people should turn back to God.
They drove out many demons, anointed many sick people with oil, and healed them.
King Herod heard about Jesus, because his name had become well known. Some people were saying, “John the Baptist has been raised from the dead, and that’s why these powers are at work in him.”
Others said, “He’s Elijah.” Still others said, “He’s a prophet, like one of the prophets long ago.”
But when Herod heard this, he said, “John, the man I beheaded, has been raised!”
Herod himself had ordered John’s arrest and put him in prison because of Herodias, his brother Philip’s wife, whom he had married.
John had told Herod, “It’s against the law for you to have your brother’s wife.”
Herodias held a grudge against John and wanted to kill him, but she couldn’t,
because Herod feared John and protected him, knowing he was righteous and holy. Herod was deeply troubled whenever he heard him, yet he liked listening to him.
Then the opportunity came. On his birthday, Herod held a dinner for his officials, military commanders, and leading men of Galilee.
Herodias’ daughter came in and danced, pleasing Herod and his guests. The king told the girl, “Ask me for whatever you want, and I’ll give it to you.”
He swore to her, “I’ll give you whatever you ask, up to half my kingdom.”
She went out and asked her mother, “What should I ask for?” Her mother said, “John the Baptist’s head.”
The girl hurried back to the king and said, “I want you to give me John the Baptist’s head on a platter right now.”
The king was deeply distressed, but because of his promises and his guests, he didn’t want to refuse her.
So he immediately sent an executioner with orders to bring John’s head. The man went and beheaded John in prison,
brought the head on a platter, and gave it to the girl, who gave it to her mother.
When John’s disciples heard what happened, they came, took his body, and laid it in a tomb.
The apostles returned to Jesus and told him everything they’d done and taught.
He said to them, “Come with me by yourselves to a quiet place and get some rest.” So many people were coming and going that they didn’t even have time to eat.
They went away in a boat by themselves to a quiet place.
But many people saw them leave and recognized them. They ran there on foot from all the towns and arrived ahead of them.
When Jesus stepped ashore, he saw a large crowd and felt compassion for them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd. So he began teaching them many things.
By now it was late in the day. His disciples came to him and said, “This is a remote place, and it’s getting late.
Send the people away so they can go to the nearby farms and villages and buy something to eat.”
But Jesus answered, “You give them something to eat.” They said, “Should we go and spend two hundred denarii on bread for them?”
He asked, “How many loaves do you have? Go check.” They found out and said, “Five—and two fish.”
Jesus told everyone to sit down in groups on the green grass.
So they sat down in groups of hundreds and fifties.
Jesus took the five loaves and two fish, looked up to heaven, gave thanks, and broke the loaves. He gave them to his disciples to hand out to the people, and he divided the two fish among them all.
Everyone ate and had enough.
The disciples collected twelve baskets full of leftover bread and fish.
Five thousand men had eaten.
Right away Jesus made his disciples get into the boat and go ahead of him to Bethsaida, while he sent the crowd away.
After saying goodbye, he went up the hillside to pray.
When evening came, the boat was out on the lake, and Jesus was alone on land.
He saw them struggling to row because the wind was against them. Around the fourth watch of the night, he came toward them, walking on the lake. He seemed about to pass them by.
When they saw him walking on the lake, they thought he was a ghost and cried out.
They all saw him and were terrified. But he immediately spoke to them: “Take courage! It’s me. Don’t be afraid.”
Then he climbed into the boat with them, and the wind died down. They were completely amazed.
They hadn’t understood what the loaves meant; their hearts were hardened.
They crossed the lake and landed at Gennesaret, where they tied up the boat.
As soon as they got out, people recognized Jesus.
They ran throughout the whole region, carrying sick people on their mats to wherever they heard he was.
Wherever he went—in villages, towns, or countryside—they laid the sick in the marketplaces and begged him to let them touch even the edge of his robe. Everyone who touched him was healed.
